newsitem.title: UK: UK Labour offers business new deal for future.
newsitem.headline: UK Labour offers business new deal for future.

text.p: Britain's main opposition Labour Party promised on Tuesday to preserve the bulk of the changes in industry and labour laws introduced in the 1980s in return for support from businessmen to tackle Britain's education and welfare needs.
In a speech to businessmen, Labour leader Tony Blair said Labour wanted to keep the more flexible labour market developed over the past 17 years of Conservative rule.
"The serious task of an incoming Labour government is not to alter what is working, but to put right what isn't," Blair said.
Blair said Labour would not be ruled by dogma or doctrine in its search for the policies needed to boost Britain's competitiveness.
In an explicit appeal to businessmen who have traditionally supported the Conservative Party, Blair offered what he called a new deal for the future.

"The deal is this: we leave intact the main changes of the 1980s in industrial relations and enterprise. And now, together, we address a new agenda for the 21st century -- education, welfare reform, infrastructure, leadership in Europe," Blair said.
Blair attacked as "risible propaganda" Conservative criticism of Labour's policy.
"Our proposals for change, including the minimum wage, would amount to less labour market regulation than in the USA," he said.

Blair said the Conservatives' deregulation agenda of the 1980s had run its course. What the British economy required now was more than just the removal of barriers to the market. It required measures to equip business and people for the future.
"This is not a choice between state control and laissez-faire. It is time to move beyond such sterile and outdated choices.

"Businesses run business. There will no "corporatism" or "picking winners". But there will be a constructive partnership between government and business in the areas where we need such a partnership to make our industry more dynamic, more competitive in the new economic world."
Blair was speaking to a Business Commission that backed Labour's proposals for a national minimum wage and the European Union's Social Chapter.
He praised the commission for being level-headed in its assessment of both issues and in appraoching them as a matter of practicality not theology.
"The truth is they are neither the promise of Nirvana that some hope, nor the end of the world as others claim," Blair said. -- +44-171-542-7767
